content: Pain was assessed in most studies using a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) ranging from 0 to 10, where 0 represented no pain at all and 10 represented the worst pain imaginable. Participants were shown pictograms corresponding to six different pain levels, with accompanying text typically translated into the local language for better understanding. Pain assessments were conducted at specific time points depending on the study design and follow-up schedule. These time points included during device placement, after placement, while wearing the device, during and after device removal, and at selected follow-up visits. Not all studies assessed pain at the same time points, so comparable time points were selected to facilitate comparisons between devices and conventional surgical circumcision. Some studies also evaluated the duration of pain experienced. For device-based circumcision methods, procedure times were calculated as the sum of preparation and procedure times for both placement and removal, excluding the time between these two events. For conventional surgery, procedure time was measured from the start of the procedure to the completion of wound dressing (first to last touch). For device application, procedure time was measured up to the end of device placement (last touch). The time required for induction of anesthesia, when used, was not included in these measurements. Device removal times were measured from the first touch to the completion of wound dressing after device removal. The World Health Organization (WHO) secretariat developed a comprehensive search strategy to identify all relevant studies, regardless of language or publication status (published, unpublished, in press, or in progress), that addressed the safety, efficacy, and acceptability of male circumcision (MC) devices. This strategy is detailed in Annex 1 on the WHO website. In addition to online searches using common electronic databases, the WHO secretariat contacted investigators known to be studying MC devices in African countries. Confidential reports of completed studies and interim reports of ongoing studies were made available to WHO for review by the Technical Advisory Group (TAG). Study investigators provided clarifications when necessary. Additional evidence on values, preferences, resource use, and costs was gathered through literature reviews in PubMed and consultations with key investigators. Stakeholders and experts within the guideline development groups were also consulted for their opinions on the acceptability of MC devices compared to surgical MC. The TAG reviewed evidence from studies on two types of devices with sufficient data to assess clinical efficacy and safety according to the WHO Framework for the clinical evaluation of male circumcision devices. The framework required initial studies to establish the safety and acceptability of the device, at least two independent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the device with an established surgical method performed by skilled providers, and at least two field studies involving relevant populations and facilities, conducted by trained mid-level or non-physician providers in settings of intended final use. Data from eligible studies were used to generate effect estimates for each priority outcome. Insufficient data were available to evaluate other devices. The quality of evidence was rated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. Evidence from RCTs was generally classified as high quality but could be downgraded due to risks of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, or publication bias. Observational studies were not formally categorized but were used to support and supplement evidence from RCTs. The WHO Guideline Steering Group, with the support of a methodologist, reviewed evidence profiles and prepared draft recommendations for consideration by the Guideline Development Group. Consensus on recommendations was achieved through email, telephone consultations, and ad hoc meetings during a sub-regional workshop in Africa. The WHO secretariat drafted the guidance, which included recommendations and programmatic considerations. Draft versions were circulated to guideline development group members, and all responses were considered in the final draft. Full consensus was achieved on the recommendations, with minimal variability resolved through small group discussions. The evidence included data on two types of devices: a collar clamp device and an elastic collar compression device. Evidence profile tables for each device, summarizing pooled data and referencing individual studies, are available in Annex 2 on the WHO website. Key points from costing studies are also included in Annex 2. Clinical studies reviewed by the TAG provided data on the safety, efficacy, and acceptability of the collar clamp device. Early studies in China demonstrated the device's safety and efficacy in participants aged 5 to 95 years when applied under local anesthesia by skilled providers. These studies formed the basis for subsequent research in African countries with public health male circumcision programs. Studies meeting the WHO Framework criteria included two initial safety and efficacy studies, two RCTs, and two field studies. These studies provided directly relevant information on the device's clinical performance in public health HIV prevention programs. In Africa, the collar clamp device was studied only in men aged 18 years and older. The African studies used a modified device design with a different mechanism for securing the outer ring. The elastic collar compression device was studied in Rwanda, Uganda, and Zimbabwe. Studies included two initial safety and efficacy studies, two RCTs, and two field studies. Interim data from two field studies in Uganda were also reviewed. All studies were conducted among men aged 18 years and older. The elastic collar compression device does not require injectable anesthesia during placement. Pain scores were difficult to compare due to evolving pain control protocols. Topical anesthetic cream containing 5% lidocaine was introduced in the Rwanda field study and adopted in subsequent studies. Pain was minimal during device placement, and most men healed within eight weeks. Healing took at least one week longer than after surgery, requiring longer sexual abstinence during the healing period.
